title: Tool Contract v1
description: The rulebook. A contract turns exactly ONE upstream REST endpoint into an MCP tool, without anyone writing server code. The shape is modeled on the Salla Admin API -- enveloped responses, scoped OAuth, standard pagination -- and Salla is the platform's primary upstream, but the format itself does not tie a contributor to it. One endpoint, one tool, one file.

contractVersion.description: Semver for THIS contract, not for the upstream API. Bumping it retires the engine's cached generated code.

kind.description: One endpoint per contract. Other kinds (multi-tool packages, openapi-import) are future work -- see the README.

interface.description: What the tool is. Maps 1:1 to the standard MCP tool declaration -- name, title, description, input schema, annotations -- plus the selection hints an agent routes on and the UI hint a client renders with.

name.description: snake_case, verb_noun. Becomes the MCP tool name, so it must be unique across the whole registry.

title.description: Human-readable display name. Served as the MCP tool's title (and as annotations.title to clients that read it there).

description.description: What the tool returns, in one sentence. The agent reads this to route.

whenToUse.description: LLM guidance, positive half: concrete situations where this tool is the right pick. Folded into the tool description and published under _meta, so every MCP client benefits.

whenNotToUse.description: LLM guidance, negative half: situations where the agent should reach for a sibling tool instead. Name the sibling.

annotations.description: MCP's core ToolAnnotations, served to clients verbatim, using MCP's exact field names. They are behavior HINTS to clients and hard facts to our gate: the schema cross-checks them against the HTTP method and the governance layer. All four are required so the author states intent explicitly -- MCP's absent-field defaults (destructiveHint true, openWorldHint true) are for clients, not for reviews. annotations.title is filled from interface.title.

readOnlyHint.description: True when the tool does not modify anything. Drives caching legality and what the agent is told about side effects.

destructiveHint.description: True when the tool may destroy or irreversibly change data (meaningful when readOnlyHint is false). Destructive tools are never cached and always need a human in the loop.

idempotentHint.description: True when calling the tool twice with the same arguments has no additional effect.

openWorldHint.description: True when the tool interacts with an open world of external entities (a live store, the internet); false for closed, self-contained computation.

allOf.$comment: A read-only tool cannot also be destructive.

schema.description: The TOOL's arguments, not the upstream's. Becomes the MCP tool's inputSchema. Expose only the parameters an agent should set -- a contract narrowing a 20-filter endpoint to three useful ones is doing its job.

forbidden.description: Argument names a caller must never be able to supply.

schema.description: Shape of the UNWRAPPED payload. Describe what is inside the envelope's data, never the envelope itself.

ui.description: How a client should display the result, when plain JSON is not the right rendering. {braces} interpolate response fields, e.g. title "Coupon {code}".

display.description: card: one record with a headline value. table: a collection, one row per item. text: a sentence. json: raw payload.

primary.description: The headline value on a card.

handler.description: A pure function run inside the engine -- no network, no token. For helpers that compute rather than fetch.

httpBinding.description: One REST endpoint on a configured upstream. The base URL is deliberately absent: the engine owns each upstream's host and credentials, so a contract cannot pin production and cannot drift when the upstream moves.

api.description: Which configured upstream the engine should call. Defaults to "salla", the platform's primary upstream. New values require the engine to be configured for that upstream first.

operationId.description: The upstream's own operationId when it publishes one (Salla does, e.g. List-Coupons). Optional, but the cheapest traceability a reviewer can get.

summary.description: The upstream's summary for the endpoint, copied so a reviewer can compare without leaving the diff.

path.description: The endpoint's path, placeholders included, e.g. /coupons/{coupon_id}.

docsUrl.description: Link to the endpoint's documentation (for Salla: docs.salla.dev), so a reviewer can check the contract against its source.

deprecation.description: Upstreams deprecate fields and endpoints on dated notices (Salla does this often). Record it here so the registry can be audited before the sunset.

scopedAuth.description: No secret is ever named in a contract. The engine resolves the credential for the target upstream at call time -- for Salla, the installing merchant's OAuth token. The contract only declares which scopes that credential must carry.

items.description: A scope in the platform's <domain>.read / <domain>.read_write convention (adopted from Salla), e.g. coupons.read.

scopes.description: Scopes the resolved credential must carry for this endpoint. For Salla, copy them from the endpoint's docs; Salla's 401 names the scopes it wanted.

requestParameters.description: How the tool's arguments become an upstream request. `name` is the wire name; `from` is the tool argument feeding it, defaulting to the same string.

path.description: Every {placeholder} in `path` needs an entry. Path parameters are always required.

mode.description: none: send no body. passthrough: every argument not consumed by path or query becomes the JSON body as-is. mapped: only the fields listed below, renamed.

allOf.$comment: mapped without fields sends an empty body, which is never what the author meant.

name.description: The name the upstream expects on the wire, e.g. coupon_id.

from.description: The tool argument to read. Omit when it matches `name`.

style.description: How an array value is serialized. Laravel-style upstreams like Salla use bracket style (status[]=a&status[]=b) unless an endpoint documents otherwise. Scalars use single.

constant.description: A fixed value always sent, instead of reading a tool argument. Use it to pin a filter the agent must not control.

allOf.$comment: A constant is not read from an argument, so pairing it with `from` is contradictory.

responseEnvelope.description: Salla-style upstreams wrap every response in an envelope ({status, success, data}) and add a pagination object on lists. The engine unwraps using this, so the agent and the UI see the payload rather than the wrapper.

dataPath.description: Dotted path to the payload inside the envelope. For Salla, always `data`.

collection.description: True when the payload is an array. Drives list rendering and tells the agent this returns many rows.

pagination.description: standard means the upstream returns a pagination object alongside the data (for Salla: {count, total, perPage, currentPage, totalPages}).

successStatuses.description: Which HTTP statuses count as success. Salla, for instance, returns 201 on some creates and 202 on deletes.

allOf.$comment: A paginated response is a collection by definition; saying otherwise misleads the agent about what it gets back.

validation.description: Guards compiled into the generated code, so a malformed argument fails locally instead of costing a round trip and an upstream 422.

match.description: Regex the argument value must match.

dependencies.description: Other contracts this tool depends on -- a lookup that must happen first, a session another binding establishes. Declared for the reviewer and the agent's documentation; the POC engine does not resolve or order them yet.

contract.description: The tool name of the contract this one depends on.

reason.description: Why the dependency exists, e.g. 'coupon ids come from list_coupons'.

governance.description: How the tool is allowed to run -- OUR policy layer, which MCP leaves open. Cross-checked by the schema against interface.annotations and the HTTP method, so policy cannot quietly disagree with declared behavior.

allOf.$comment: propose-apply exists so a human can approve. Requiring the mode without the approval is a governance hole.
A cacheable result with no TTL never expires, so stale store data would be served indefinitely.

annotationGovernanceRules.$comment: Cross-layer rules tying the MCP annotations to the governance policy. A hint that lies to clients while policy quietly does the opposite is worse than either mistake alone.

allOf.$comment: A destructive tool must never be cacheable. Caching a write is a correctness bug, not a preference.

Only a read-only tool may be cacheable. Without this, a write could be marked cacheable and merely happen not to be cached because the engine checks readOnlyHint too -- an invariant enforced in one place and silently contradicted in another.

methodGovernanceRules.$comment: Cross-layer rules tying the HTTP verb and its scopes to the MCP annotations. These catch the mistakes that matter: a write tool marked read-only would be cached and served stale, and a read tool asking for read_write hands the store more access than the job needs.

allOf.$comment: GET is a read. Marking it otherwise disables caching for no reason and misleads the agent.
POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE change store data. None of them is read-only.
DELETE removes real data. It is destructive whatever the author felt about it, and always gets a human in the loop.
Least privilege: a read-only tool must not request a read_write scope. Grants are made per app installation, so an over-broad ask gives the whole app more power over a store than this tool needs.
The converse: a tool that writes cannot do it with a read-only scope. The upstream would reject the call at runtime; better to reject the contract at review time.
